description: We are a passionate team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.” Our goal is to build a web application that unifies satellite fire data, visualizes historical fire activity, and detects unusual patterns. Our team combines Backend Development, AI, Data Analysis, and Business Analysis to transform NASA data into meaningful insights.
summary:
OnFire brings two different satellite perspectives together to make active fire data easier to explore and understand. Using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS observations, the platform allows users to examine hotspot distribution and changes in fire activity across Punjab, India, during October–November 2025.

By presenting both datasets in one interactive environment, OnFire helps users explore where observations overlap, where they differ, and how satellite resolution and observation characteristics affect the picture of fire activity.

Instead of treating each satellite dataset separately, OnFire offers a clearer, more accessible way to investigate their complementary observations. The goal is to support better understanding of satellite-based fire monitoring data and make it easier to explore patterns that may otherwise be difficult to see.
details:
OnFire is a web-based platform that brings NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot observations into one interactive environment. It helps users explore fire activity, compare observations from two satellite instruments with different spatial resolutions, and understand their differences.

The project focuses on Punjab, India, using NASA FIRMS data collected between October 20 and November 30, 2025. Our workflow includes data acquisition, cleaning, geographic filtering, validation, database storage, and interactive visualization through a web interface.

Users can explore hotspot locations, examine observations over time, and compare MODIS and VIIRS data through the platform's available visualization features.

OnFire aims to make satellite fire data more accessible and understandable, supporting researchers, environmental analysts, and other users interested in monitoring agricultural burning and fire activity.

The backend was developed using C# and ASP.NET Core, with a database and data importer pipeline. The frontend uses web technologies for interactive visualization. The project also uses Python for data processing and analysis. The exact frameworks and libraries are documented in the project source code.

Our approach focuses on combining different satellite perspectives in one platform while considering data quality, spatial resolution differences, observation timing, and the limitations of hotspot detection.
